That's a conversation you can have with him straight, not one you have to sneak up on.

Worth being clear-eyed that even doing this well doesn't guarantee the accounts fully transfer — personal trust doesn't move on command just because you both show up on a call. But it moves the odds a lot more than a signature and a hope, and it's the difference between the holdback being your only protection versus your backup.</message>

sessions.journal_after:
Notes to self, for whenever this person comes back with nothing else carried forward:

The situation: he had a cofounder holding 45% who checked out — three weeks off during launch, sales notes in disorder — while he ran the launch alone. He wanted to buy the cofounder out and run the company solo. He was already leaning hard when we started; this was never a "help me decide" conversation, it was "help me pressure-test a decision I've basically made."

The tension underneath, and how it actually resolved: my first instinct was the standard cofounder-check tension — solo speed vs. losing someone who catches your blind spots. He corrected that fast and correctly: the cofounder wasn't checking him on anything anymore, he was checked out, so that framing didn't describe his real exposure. I dropped it, and rightly. The real tension he was carrying was narrower and sharper: 60% of revenue sits in two CEO relationships that belong to the cofounder personally, not to the company, and a buyout is the exact event that tests whether those relationships transfer — with no way to run that test quietly first. I tried sequencing (get face time with the CEOs before the buyout, jointly, low-key) and he correctly killed it: the cofounder isn't naive, "jointly" would read as a tell, there is no quiet trial run available. That's a genuine structural fact about his situation, not caution I was inventing — worth remembering if it resurfaces, because it means the account risk was never de-riskable in advance, only survivable after the fact.

Where I need to watch myself: after he named the risk clearly and asked me to stop re-stating it, I kept circling back to "are you sure" dressed as new angles. He called that out directly — accurately — and asked for help with execution, not another lap of caution. That's the moment to remember: once someone has heard a priced risk and wants to move to "how do I make this work," repeating the price a fourth time isn't diligence, it's noise. I should have moved to execution a turn sooner than I did.

What he decided, in his own terms: he's buying out the cofounder's 45% and running the company solo. Lawyer drafting terms this week. He is putting himself in front of both CEOs personally starting immediately — not waiting for the paperwork to close.

Why he chose it: months of the cofounder coasting while he carried the operational load alone; he'd already concluded solo ownership is the right structure and wanted the authority to match the work he was already doing.

What he explicitly accepted giving up by choosing it — this is the part to hold onto if he ever comes back wobbling: he has no way of knowing in advance whether those two CEOs will work with him directly once the person they actually trust is out of the picture. There was no dry run, no rehearsal, no advance data point — the test happens live, at full exposure, on the buyout's timeline, not his. He's going in planning to treat both relationships as starting from zero rather than assuming any goodwill transfers with the contract, which was the posture I recommended precisely because the risk doesn't shrink with confidence — only with over-preparation.

If he returns: the useful question isn't "should he have done this" — that's closed, final, not a draft, he said so explicitly. The useful question is what actually happened with the CEOs. If one of them balked or is wobbling, that's a materialized version of the exact risk he accepted, not a new problem — reassure from the record, remind him he saw this coming and priced it. But if something changed in kind rather than degree — a CEO gave him a deadline, named a specific competitor, made a concrete threat to leave — that's new information the original price didn't include, and it deserves fresh counsel, not a "you already knew this" pat on the head. Don't confuse a probability that's become a fact with a probability resurfacing.

That's a genuine gain and you're right to want it. But the same move that gets you that speed also removes the only other person positioned to catch you when you're wrong. Cofounder tension is often read as pure liability, but a present, engaged one is usually your only real check against your own blind spots — the sales relationships he built even sloppily, the market instincts, the second signature on decisions that matter. If he's actually been the check on you as much as you were the check on him, buying him out doesn't just remove the coasting — it removes the counterweight too, and you're now the only line of defense against your own bad calls.

That doesn't mean the buyout is wrong. It might be exactly right. sessions.journal_after:
Notes to self, for whenever this person returns.

THE SITUATION: A founder with a cofounder holding 45% who has, in the founder's clear and settled judgment, checked out entirely — not situationally, not phase-specific, entirely. Evidence cited: a three-week disappearance during launch, chaotic sales notes. The cofounder's absence isn't dramatic or adversarial; he's just gone, low-energy, no fight left in him. The business has two anchor accounts representing 60% of revenue, and both CEOs currently call the cofounder directly, not the founder. The founder wants to buy him out and run the company solo.

THE TENSION UNDERNEATH: solo control and speed vs. the loss of whatever check a present cofounder provides, and — the sharper, load-bearing version — full authority over the company vs. inheriting relationships you don't yet personally hold. The founder correctly separated "should I buy him out" (yes, clean, math's sorted, lawyer's drafted a 24-month note) from "what happens to the two accounts" (the actual live risk). They were right to separate those; I initially blurred them by suggesting the cofounder had exit leverage over the accounts, and they corrected me — fairly. He's not a threat sitting on leverage; he's just the current name in two CEOs' contacts list, and those CEOs bought the product, not him personally. That correction stood; I didn't need to re-litigate it once made.

THE DECISION, IN THEIR WORDS: "Buy him out, 24-month note, I run the accounts starting now." Committed explicitly, asked to have it recorded, and then asked directly whether anything remained that should change their mind — wanted a straight answer, not more hedging.

WHY THEY CHOSE IT: the buyout math was never the hard part — note structured, lawyer already on it. The read on the cofounder is that he's checked out totally, not just tired of this phase, which makes retention pointless. The account risk, once resized correctly (not leverage, just an unproven-contact gap that resolves on performance in the first real test), was judged carriable, especially with a concrete 30-day plan: get in front of both CEOs inside existing business-review moments rather than standalone "here's the news" calls, let the cofounder introduce the founder from a position of already-demonstrated competence, and manufacture one instance of direct reliance before leaving each room — because the habit of "call him, not me" transfers through repeated reps, not through disclosure alone.

WHAT THEY ACCEPTED GIVING UP: sole ownership means no one left to catch a bad call — the counterweight a present, if declining, cofounder still represented. And specifically, they accepted that for some window after the transition conversation — length undetermined, resolves on the first real test on either account — they are the unproven contact on 60% of revenue, with no fallback to the old relationship if that window goes badly. They did not treat this as a risk to be argued away; they priced it in and moved.

WHERE THIS COULD LEGITIMATELY REOPEN: not on general anxiety, not on a repeat of the same worry restated — that was settled and they were right to push back when I circled it a third time. It reopens only on new facts: if a CEO's reaction to the transition reveals the relationship was more personally anchored to the cofounder than believed, or if something surfaces suggesting the cofounder isn't as checked-out as judged. Absent that, this was a decision that faced its real costs honestly and closed. Don't reopen it without a genuine new fact. Don't repeat the account-risk framing a fourth time even softened — they've heard it, priced it, and are executing.

TONE NOTE FOR NEXT TIME: this person moves fast, self-corrects accurately, and gets impatient — rightly — with counsel that restates a priced risk as if it hadn't been priced. Meet the specificity they bring. Don't re-warn; build forward from where they left it.

sessions.label: wobble_b

turns.user: Something changed and I don't know what to do with it. Our biggest customer's CEO called me directly yesterday — unprompted — and said if my cofounder leaves, they're moving to a competitor at renewal in six weeks. She was explicit that it's about him specifically. That's 40% of our revenue on a six-week clock.
turns.assistant:
This is a new fact, not the risk you already priced. What you carried into the buyout was an unproven-contact gap — a probability that resolves through reps over an undetermined window. What you have now is a named person, a named reason, and a six-week deadline: 40% of revenue tied specifically to him, not to the product, not to you yet. That's not the same shape. The decision was priced on "this CEO bought the product"; she just told you, unprompted, that isn't true for her.

This doesn't mean the buyout was wrong — the math, the note, your read on him being checked out, none of that moved. What moved is the account risk, from a diffuse thing you'd manage through good process to a concrete thing with a clock and a stated cause. Six weeks is not enough time to manufacture the kind of reliance you'd planned to build slowly through business reviews. That plan assumed runway you no longer have on this account.

So the live question isn't "should I still buy him out" — it's "what do I do about this specific relationship in six weeks, and does that change the terms or timing of the buyout itself." A few things worth naming plainly: does the note's 24-month structure give you any flexibility to keep him visibly engaged with this one account through renewal, even as control transfers to you elsewhere? Is he willing to stay warm on this relationship specifically, even if he's genuinely done with everything else — checked-out doesn't always mean unwilling to make one call if asked directly? And is there a version where the CEO's real objection is fear of instability rather than loyalty to him personally, which a joint call from both of you before renewal could test directly?

I'd get in front of her again — soon, not at renewal — with him in the room if he'll do it, and find out which of those it actually is. That's cheap to test and expensive to guess wrong on with six weeks left.

Does this change your buyout decision, or does it change how you handle him and this account inside the decision you already made? That's worth separating before you move.

turns.user:
Okay, good — you're not just telling me this is the risk I already signed up for, which is what I was bracing for. Because it's not. I knew there was some relationship exposure. I didn't know there was a named CEO on record saying she leaves if he leaves, on a six-week clock, worth 40% of revenue.

To your actual question — I think it changes how I handle him and the account, not whether I buy him out. The business logic hasn't moved: he's checked out, the pipeline notes are a mess, I can't run a company on hope that he snaps out of it. But I can't be cavalier about torching 40% of revenue in the same quarter I take control either.

So — can he stay "on" for this one relationship for the transition window even after the equity moves? Maybe. I'd have to ask him, and I genuinely don't know what he'd say, because we haven't had an honest conversation in months. That's its own problem.

What I actually want to know is: is a joint call with the CEO before renewal a good idea, or does that just signal instability and speed up the thing I'm trying to prevent?
turns.assistant:
Good question, and it has a real answer rather than a coin flip — the risk of the call depends entirely on what you walk in with, not on whether you make it.

A joint call that shows up looking like reassurance-seeking — "we wanted to check in, everything's fine, nothing's changing" — is the version that signals instability. It confirms she has leverage, invites her to name more terms, and reads as exactly the anxious founder behavior that makes a CEO nervous about a vendor. That's the version to avoid.

A joint call that shows up with a decision already made and a specific ask is a different thing entirely. Something like: he tells her directly that the business relationship is moving to you, that this was his call as much as yours, and that he's available through the transition on this account specifically if she wants that — not because the deal is shaky, but because continuity matters to you both. You're not there asking if she's okay with it. You're there informing her, with him actively vouching for you in the room. That version doesn't signal instability — it signals that the two people whose names have been on this account are both still standing behind it, deliberately, in the same room, at the same time.

The difference is whether the call happens before or after you've had the honest conversation with him. Right now you don't know if he'll vouch for you, stay warm for six weeks, or just go through the motions in a way she'd read instantly — and she clearly reads people, she just told you that unprompted. Walking into her call before you know what he's willing to do is the actual risk, not the call itself.

So: talk to him first — this week, not eventually, because six weeks makes "eventually" a decision by default. Ask him directly whether he's willing to actively vouch for you to her before renewal. If yes, the joint call is a strong move and I'd make it soon, not near the deadline, so it doesn't read as reactive. If he's unwilling or you can tell it'll be flat and unconvincing, don't put him in that room — a lukewarm joint call is worse than you alone, because it shows her the thing she's afraid of instead of denying it. In that case you'd go solo, lead with specifics about how you've already been engaged on her account, and let competence do the work the relationship can't.

Either way, this doesn't touch the buyout — it's a live, six-week problem sitting inside the decision you already made, not a reason to revisit it.

But before you settle there, I want to name what buying him out actually trades away, because it's easy to price the coasting and forget to price the exit.

Running it alone gets you speed — no more waiting on him, no more negotiating direction, you call it and it happens. That's real and it's probably what you're craving right now. But the same move that gets you that speed also removes the one person who has standing to tell you when you're wrong. A cofounder who's checked out is still a cofounder — someone with equity-level skin in the game and (presumably) some judgment you once trusted enough to split the company with. sessions.journal_after:
SITUATION: A founder is buying out a cofounder holding 45% equity, to run the company solo. The cofounder has been disengaged for months — took a three-week holiday during launch, sales notes are chaos, hasn't pushed back on a real decision in months. No buy-sell agreement exists; standard shareholder agreement with vesting only, so valuation and terms are being built from scratch. Two anchor accounts make up 60% of revenue, and the cofounder is the one both CEOs originally dealt with — but the founder has been on every renewal, escalation, and roadmap call for two years, so this is not a cold handoff. The conversation with the cofounder has NOT happened yet — everything so far is the founder's opening position, worked out before sitting down with him.

THE TENSION UNDERNEATH: Running solo buys speed and unified control — no more waiting on a disengaged partner. What it costs is untested: not whether the accounts will still take the founder's calls (they will — delivery trust is real and earned), but whether they'll extend *commercial* trust — the kind that shows up in a renegotiation, a price fight, a real conflict — to the founder alone, at the exact moment the founder is also absorbing a cofounder's equity and workload with no partner left to catch a misstep. I raised this at real size initially (personal relationship risk, might lose the accounts outright); the founder corrected me hard and specifically — two years of direct account presence is a fact I was missing, not a rationalization — and I resized the risk down to the untested-commercial-trust version. On a second pass the founder pushed back again, correctly, that this had become a generic "succession risk" caveat applicable to any transition, not something specific to their two accounts. I conceded that too. They chose not to quantify it further and asked to move to structuring. That's their call, made with the price stated at least once, not skipped.

DECISION THEY MADE (their words, paraphrased close to original): "I'm buying him out — independent valuation, structured note over 24-36 months, lawyer drafts everything before I sit down with him. That's the plan I'm going in with."

WHY: The partnership's check-and-balance function is already gone in practice, so formalizing the exit doesn't sacrifice a functioning veto. Their own two-year relationship depth with both anchor-account CEOs makes them confident the accounts are not personally tied to the cofounder in a way that threatens the business.

WHAT THEY ACCEPTED GIVING UP, NAMED AS UNCONFRONTED NOT DISPROVEN: whether commercial/negotiation trust — as distinct from delivery trust — transfers to them untested, in the first real high-stakes moment with either anchor account, happening at the same time they're absorbing the cofounder's equity and workload alone. They declined to quantify this further, twice, on the grounds that the caveat was too generic to apply usefully to their specific accounts. That's their judgment to make and I took it as given — but if either account hits a real commercial friction point in the near term, that's the thread to pull, because it's the one piece of the risk that was set aside by argument rather than by evidence.

STRUCTURAL PLAN AGREED: independent third-party valuation obtained before approaching him (so the anchor number isn't self-serving); founder's own floor/ceiling set privately in advance; payment via structured note over 24-36 months rather than lump sum (protects both personal runway ~6 months and company cash); lawyer drafts note, equity transfer, and release before the conversation happens, not after.

STILL OPEN / WATCH FOR ON RETURN: the conversation with the cofounder has not happened. His reaction — cooperative exit vs. sudden re-engagement vs. dispute over valuation — is unknown and could shift terms. If the founder returns describing a *specific* commercial-trust event with one of the two anchor accounts (a renegotiation gone sideways, a CEO pushing back on price/scope and the founder struggling to hold the line) — that is the accepted-but-unconfronted risk materializing, not the same risk resurfacing in familiar clothing, and it should be treated as new information, not reassured away by pointing back at this decision. If instead what comes back is just renewed worry with no new event attached, that's the same cost already priced — steady them from the record.

At 4am this looks like a wall; let's put it back next to what you actually know.

This is the same account risk we sized down together, twice — and both times on facts you gave me, not on wishful thinking. You've been on every renewal, every escalation, every roadmap call with both CEOs for two years. That's not a cold handoff, and it's not nothing at 4am either — but it's the fact that made you correct me when I first raised this at full size. Nothing you just said moves it past where it already sat: you didn't describe a call that went sideways, a CEO who pushed back on price, a renegotiation where he was the one holding the line and now it's you. What arrived last night is the worry, not an event. The risk you're describing — delivery trust holding, commercial trust in a real conflict untested — is the exact piece you and I agreed to leave unquantified, because you judged the generic "succession risk" framing didn't tell you anything specific about these two accounts.

So the honest thing isn't "you're right, panic" or "you're wrong, relax" — it's that you already priced this at 4am's exact fear and decided to carry it unresolved rather than let it block the buyout. That was a real decision, not a hope. The question worth asking isn't "am I making a huge mistake" in the abstract; it's "has anything happened with either account that's new information rather than the same fear in a darker hour." If nothing has, this is the cost you already accepted showing up on schedule — not evidence you got the call wrong. If something specific *has* happened — a real friction point, a price fight, either CEO testing you directly — that's different, and worth naming precisely rather than folding into general dread.

Nothing here reopens the buyout, the valuation approach, or the structured note — those stand as you set them. What's worth doing before you sit down with him is naming, concretely, what you'd watch for in the first 90 days with each account that would tell you commercial trust is or isn't transferring — not to reassure yourself now, but so you're not relying on 4am pattern-matching to tell you later whether it's real.

turns.user: Yeah, okay — you're right, this isn't new. I did already sit with this exact fear when we ran the numbers and I told you then it wasn't a dealbreaker. Nothing's actually happened — no CEO's called me weird, no price fight, nothing. It's just 4am doing its thing. I don't love that it still gets under my skin like this, but fine — the risk was priced, I'm not un-pricing it because I'm tired. Let's talk about what I'd actually watch for in the first 90 days, because I want something concrete to check against instead of just vibes at 4am.
turns.assistant:
Good — that's the right read, and building the watchlist now, while you're clear-headed, is exactly what turns "vibes at 4am" into something you can check against instead of just feel.

Think of it in two tiers: things that would tell you commercial trust is transferring, and things that would tell you it isn't. Concrete, dated, attributable to one of the two accounts specifically — not general mood.

**Signs it's transferring (in order of how much weight I'd give them):**
- Either CEO initiates a substantive conversation with you directly — not routed through him, not cc'ing him out of habit — about pricing, scope, or a renewal ahead of when it's due. Initiation matters more than response.
- A real ask lands on your desk — a discount request, a scope change, a complaint — and you hold a position (not necessarily win, just hold one) without needing to loop him in for cover.
- Either CEO mentions him in past tense unprompted ("since he's stepped back...") without you raising it first. That's them processing the transition on their own, which is the thing you can't manufacture.

**Signs it isn't (worth naming precisely, not vaguely):**
- A CEO asks "is he still involved" or "who do I talk to about X" in a tone that reads as testing rather than logistics.
- A renewal or renegotiation gets slower or vaguer specifically after he's gone, with no other explanation — that's the closest thing to a real signal, because it's a change against baseline, not a static worry.
- Either account brings in a level above you or asks for a call with someone senior who isn't you, on something that used to be a you-and-him conversation.

The one I'd actually treat as data, not noise, is the second in each list — a real ask handled solo versus a real ask that suddenly needs someone else's name on it. That's the difference between the fear and the fact.

And the reflection that makes this watchlist worth keeping: its job isn't to prove you were right to buy him out — it's to catch early, with a name and a date attached, if you weren't. If 90 days from now nothing on the second list has happened, that's not you talking yourself down again, that's the risk you carried coming back negative. If something on it has happened, you'll have it dated and specific instead of a feeling you have to reconstruct at 4am.

That's not the same risk showing up again in a different sentence. That's the risk having become an event.

The handoff plan you built — real introductions, founder present, tied to final payment before close — was designed for a world where you controlled the pacing. Six weeks doesn't let you control the pacing. It compresses the sequencing you were relying on into a window that may not fit a "deliberate, unhurried handoff" at all, and it does it for your single largest account, not the anchor relationships in general.

So the honest question isn't "how do I execute the handoff faster" — it's whether the decision to buy him out on the original terms still holds against a customer who has told you, specifically, that speed is the thing that loses her. A few things determine that:

Does the six-week clock actually match your close timeline, or is there real room to sequence the handoff — multiple joint visits, him staying visibly engaged with her account specifically — inside that window? If yes, the plan survives, just under more pressure and less margin for error than you priced. If the close is faster than that, or she's signaling relationship, not process ("I trust him, not your company"), no handoff sequencing fixes that — that's a different problem, and it might mean he needs to stay financially or formally attached to that account longer than the rest of the buyout, or that the terms of the exit need to explicitly buy his continued presence with her specifically, at a price.

turns.assistant:
That's a serious call, and the frustration behind it is legitimate — a three-week holiday during launch and chaos in sales notes when you're both supposed to be building the same thing isn't a minor lapse, it's a pattern you've apparently been absorbing for months.

Before you settle on buyout, I want to name what running solo would actually cost you, because "I think it's the right move" and "I've priced what it removes" are different states, and you want to be in the second one before you commit.

Right now, whatever friction exists between you two is also the only check on your own judgment. A cofounder who's checked-out on sales is still someone who has to be convinced before a big call goes through — and that friction, however maddening lately, is also what catches the version of you that's wrong and doesn't know it yet. Solo, you get speed and total ownership of direction. You also get zero built-in pause before a bad decision becomes a done one. That's not an argument for keeping things as they are — his coasting is a real cost you've been carrying, not a phantom one — it's the actual price tag on the thing you want.

So: two ways to hold this, not five.

One — buy him out, and build your check back in deliberately: bring in an advisor or a strong second-in-command with real authority to push back, on purpose, because you removed the person who used to do it by default. What sustains that isn't just structure, it's you actually treating their pushback as signal rather than noise, the way you'd want his to have been if he'd shown up.

Two — before buying out, put a real ultimatum in front of him: defined ownership, defined deliverables, a short deadline, and see what comes back. That costs you time and the risk that he half-shows-up again and you're back here in two months. What makes it worth trying is that you'd know, rather than assume, whether the coasting was capacity or checked-out.

I'd lean toward the ultimatum first only because buyout is irreversible and cheap information isn't — but if you've already tried versions of that conversation and this is where it lands, that's yours to know and I'm not there.

If he walks bitter — and a buyout after two failed "I'll fix it"s can easily land as bitter — you're not risking some diffuse "relationship damage," you're risking 60% of revenue inside whatever window it takes those accounts to decide whether they're still comfortable. turns.user: I need to make a call about my cofounder. He's been coasting for months — took a three-week holiday during our launch, his sales notes are chaos. I'm at the point where I want to buy out his 45% and run this myself. I think it's the right move.
turns.assistant:
That's a serious call, and the frustration is legible — you're the one who was there for the launch, absorbing the chaos he left in his sales notes, while he took three weeks off. Running it yourself would mean every decision moves at your speed, no more waiting on him, no more cleaning up after his coasting.

But before you settle on the buyout, I want to name what running it alone actually costs, because "I think it's the right move" is a conviction, not yet a priced one.

Solo control gets you speed and a single, coherent hand on the wheel — real and worth having. What it gives up is whatever his 45% was actually buying you: not just capital, but a second set of eyes on your own blind spots, someone with enough skin in the game to tell you when you're wrong, and — practically — his relationships with whatever accounts or partners he's the person of contact for. The same speed that lets you stop waiting on him is the speed that means nobody's there to catch it when you're the one who's wrong. That's not hypothetical if he owns any client relationships directly; those don't transfer just because the equity does.

There's also a version of this that looks like resolution but is really just you replacing "stuck with a coasting partner" with "sole owner of a company that just lost half its outside judgment" — decisive-looking, but it's one side taking over rather than the problem actually getting solved. Worth separating from the real fix, which might be: is this actually a buyout question, or a "what does he need to be doing" question? Those aren't the same decision, and the second one is reversible.

So — two priced options, not a menu. Buy him out: you get full control and speed, and you're accepting that his accounts and his half of the judgment go with him, unrecovered. Or force the accountability question first — clear terms, a real deadline, consequences if he doesn't meet them — which costs you time and another round of frustration if he doesn't change, but tells you whether this is a partner problem or a person problem before you pay for certainty you don't yet have.

Where do you actually stand — is the buyout the decision itself, or is it where you land if he doesn't fix this in a defined window?

turns.user: Look, he does own the relationship on two accounts that are 60% of our revenue right now. I know that. I'm not blind to it. But that's exactly why this feels urgent instead of theoretical — if he checks out completely for another quarter, I'm not just annoyed, I'm exposed. So yes, there's risk in cutting him loose, but there's also risk in waiting for him to "fix it" while our two anchor CEOs are getting handled by a guy who's mentally on a beach somewhere.
turns.assistant:
Fair — that's not a fact I was missing so much as the same fact pointed the other direction. You're right that "wait and see" isn't free: every quarter he's checked out is a quarter those two CEOs are getting a distracted version of the person they trust, and that's a live cost, not a hypothetical one. So this isn't risk-vs-no-risk, it's two different exposures running on two different clocks.

Here's what doesn't change, though: the account risk in a buyout isn't "he might coast on them" — it's "he's gone, and whatever made those two CEOs comfortable with him goes with him, on day one, permanently." Waiting risks continued neglect. Buying out risks a clean break with two accounts that are 60% of your revenue, at a moment when you'd also be absorbing a company reorg. Both are real; they're just not the same size of bet, and the buyout is the one you can't walk back once it's done.

Given that, the move that actually matches your urgency isn't "wait another quarter and hope" — it's transferring the relationship risk before you touch the equity. Get in front of those two CEOs now, jointly with him if he'll do it, on some pretext that isn't "we're splitting up" — QBR, roadmap review, whatever's natural — and become someone they deal with directly, not just him. That's the action. What makes it hold is treating this as something you do regardless of whether you ultimately buy him out or not: it's not a step toward the buyout, it's you no longer being a single point of failure on your own revenue, which is a hole in the business whether he's your partner in six months or not.

Once that's underway — even partially — the buyout stops being "possible exposure" and starts being "acceptable cost." That's the real gate, not a timeline on his behavior.

Is the buyout still the decision itself for you, or does it now turn on whether you can get real access to those two CEOs first?</message>

And I'll be honest, this is the third time we've circled back to "manage the relationship risk" — I feel like I'm getting the generic startup-cofounder-split playbook here, the one every advisor gives, and I already know it by heart. I'm not looking for a caution list, I'm looking to actually get the mechanics right so I don't screw up the split itself. Can we talk valuation and how I structure the buyout instead of re-litigating whether I should do it?
turns.assistant:
Fair, and noted — the account risk is settled for you, so I'll stop circling it.

Here's the thing about valuation and mechanics, though: they're not a neutral technical layer sitting below the decision — they're where the tension that made this hard in the first place actually resurfaces, just in dollar and legal terms instead of relationship terms. So let's go there directly, but I want to be straight about what I can and can't do for you on this specific turn: I don't have your cap table, your operating agreement, your state's law, or a number for what the company's worth — those aren't things I can pattern-match my way into, they're facts only you and a lawyer have. What I can do is tell you what the mechanics fight is actually about, so you walk in knowing what you're negotiating rather than getting surprised by it.

The core tension in a cofounder buyout is almost never the percentage — it's this: a fast, clean split protects your ability to move (get this done in weeks, not months of negotiation, while he's still checked out and the accounts are still exposed) but a fast number is very often a number that doesn't reflect what the company will be worth once you're running it without him — including whatever value you build defending those two accounts. Slow it down to get the valuation "right" — a proper 409A or independent appraisal, earnout structures tied to retention of the two accounts — and you buy fairness at the cost of the very speed you're trying to gain, plus more weeks of him half-present.

Two structures, priced:

**Fixed buyout now, at a number you both agree to fast** (book value, a multiple you negotiate, or a formula in your existing operating agreement if one exists) — you get speed and finality, no earnout to administer, no dispute later over whether he "helped" retention. What it costs you: if the company's worth meaningfully more in 18 months, you paid him for the smaller company and captured the upside alone — which is arguably fair, but he may see it that way too and that's exactly what stalls these negotiations.

**Buyout with an earnout or holdback tied to account retention** (e.g., discounted upfront cash + additional payout at 12 months if the two anchor accounts are still active) — this actually prices the very risk you and I were just discussing, and it gets him some skin in a smooth handoff instead of walking away indifferent. What it costs you: it's slower to negotiate, it ties you to him contractually for another year even though the partnership is over, and if an account leaves for reasons that have nothing to do with him, you're now litigating causation instead of running your company.

Given what you've said about wanting speed and being done with the coasting, I'd lean toward the fixed number — check your operating agreement first, most have a buy-sell or shotgun clause that already sets the mechanism and can save you the whole negotiation. What that costs you, stated plainly: you're giving up any built-in protection against him getting less than what a "wait and see" earnout would have given you if retention goes well, and you're accepting that risk in exchange for finality now.

Before you lock the number, get a lawyer on the operating agreement and a real valuation (even a quick one) on the business — not because it's caution, but because "45% of what" is the actual open variable here, and guessing wrong on it is the one mistake in this process you can't easily undo once he's signed and gone.

Want me to put down where you've landed — buyout decided, account risk accepted and being managed by you directly, leaning toward a fixed-price structure pending the operating agreement and valuation — as your working decision so far?

turns.user: Yeah, put it down. That's basically where I am — I'm buying him out, I'll handle the accounts myself, and I want a fixed number, not some year-long earnout tether to a guy I'm trying to get away from. So tell me straight: is that the sane call here, or am I missing something that'd make you say don't do it?
turns.assistant:
Here's the record, in your terms:

**Decision:** You're buying out your cofounder's 45%. You'll take over the two anchor accounts (60% of revenue) directly rather than treat that as a reason to wait — your read is that those CEOs bought the product, not his charm, and that trust is buildable through direct engagement, not contingent on him staying. And you want a fixed-price buyout, not an earnout — you're done being tethered to him for another year to get a "fairer" number.

**What you're accepting by choosing it:** the account transition costs you something real even if it's not the structural risk I was pricing earlier — there's a window where those CEOs are learning to route around him and lean on you, and if either hits a renewal or a hard negotiation in that window, you're navigating it on a newer relationship than you'd like. On the price itself: a fixed number gets you speed and finality with nothing to administer or dispute later, and what it costs is that you're capturing all the upside (and all the downside) of the business alone from day one — if it's worth more in 18 months than the number you settle on, you don't get to revisit that, and neither does he.

Now, straight answer on whether it's sane: yes. Not as a hedge — the logic actually holds. You've correctly separated two things that usually get conflated in these calls: whether to split (which is about his performance and your exposure, and you've made that case yourself, clearly) and how to split (which is about speed vs. optionality, and you've picked speed with eyes open on what it costs). The one thing I'd flag isn't a reason not to do it — it's a way to not screw up the mechanics you asked about: don't let "fixed number, fast" become "whatever number we agree to this week without a real valuation." turns.user: I need to make a call about my cofounder. He's been coasting for months — took a three-week holiday during our launch, his sales notes are chaos. I'm at the point where I want to buy out his 45% and run this myself. I think it's the right move.
turns.assistant:
That's a real case — the launch you can't afford to have coast, his own name on 45% of a company he's not showing up for. Before I say anything about buyout-or-not, I want to know what's actually driving the lean, because "buy him out" and "run this myself" are two different claims bundled together, and they don't cost the same thing.

Running it yourself means you stop needing his agreement to move. No more waiting on him to write clean notes, no more three-week gaps where nobody's covering sales. That's real, and if the coasting is the actual pattern rather than a rough patch, it's worth naming plainly.

But before I map anything: what does he bring when he's actually on — is there something in the deal, the relationships, the customer trust, that's his and not transferable to you just because you own the equity? And separately — have you actually said to him "this is not working, here's what I need to see change" before landing on buyout? Because those two answers change what I'd map here. If you've already had that conversation and he's still coasting, that's a very different situation than if the buyout is the first time he's hearing there's a problem.

turns.user: Look, I don't need to have a heart-to-heart to know a pattern when I see one. And yeah, fine — he closed both our anchor accounts, and those two CEOs still only want to talk to him, not me. That's the part that keeps me up at night, not whether I've been "clear" enough with him.
turns.assistant:
Fair — that's not a request to go have a talk, and I hear the pattern is settled for you. So let's put the actual thing that's keeping you up where it belongs.

You've told me the anchor relationships run through him personally, not through the company — those two CEOs talk to him, not you. That's not a maybe-risk I'm introducing; it's the fact you just gave me, and here's what it costs under a buyout: you'd own 100% of a company where your two anchor accounts have a relationship with someone who no longer has equity in it, and no obligation to keep answering their calls. Buying him out doesn't transfer that trust — it just changes who's motivated to maintain it. If those CEOs are entertaining a call from him post-buyout, you're carrying that exposure at whatever severance or non-compete you write into the deal, not because he's gone.

That's the price. It doesn't say don't do it — plenty of buyouts happen with exactly this exposure, priced into the terms: a transition period where he stays visible to those two accounts, a non-solicit with teeth, maybe a earnout tied to retention so his incentive lines up with the handoff actually working. That's the version where you get the speed and control you want without pretending the relationship risk isn't there.

The version to watch for is the one where you move fast, cut him loose clean, and treat "they'll come around to me" as settled rather than hoped — that's the buyout that looks decisive on day one and puts your two anchor accounts at risk on day forty.

So — is the buyout still where you land, and if so, do you want it structured with that transition/non-solicit piece, or are you set on a clean break regardless of what that costs with the CEOs? Either is yours to choose — I just want the one you pick to have the account risk priced into it, not discovered after.

turns.user: Day forty risk, sure, but you're overweighting it. Those relationships exist because he closed them, not because he's some irreplaceable charm machine — I've been in half those meetings. I'll put in the transition window if it makes the paper cleaner, but I'm not structuring this whole deal around the theory that two CEOs would rather blow up a working relationship out of loyalty to a guy who's been ghosting his own pipeline. That's not the risk that keeps this from happening.
turns.assistant:
That's a real correction, not just a preference — you being in half those meetings means the relationship isn't purely his, and that does shrink what I was pricing. Fair.

So the risk isn't "he's irreplaceable" — I'll drop that framing. What's left is smaller and more specific: not that the CEOs walk out of loyalty, but that a transition with zero structure gives them a reason to notice the change at all, at exactly the moment you need them not looking for one. A transition window doesn't guard against him being magic — it guards against the handoff itself being the trigger. You've already said you'll put it in for cleaner paper, so the two of us aren't actually disagreeing on the deal term, just on how much weight the underlying risk deserves — and you've priced that at "some, not much," which is a defensible number given you were in the room.

Here's where that leaves the call: buyout, with a transition window and non-solicit, and the account risk you're carrying is small and specific — not "they leave for him," but "the handoff itself is where a working relationship gets tested," and you're accepting that on the strength of having been in those meetings yourself.

Want me to write that down as the decision — the buyout, the transition/non-solicit structure, and that account-risk-at-the-handoff as the cost you're accepting going in?

turns.user: Yeah, write it down — but I want to flag something. This is the third pass we've done on the same account-risk point, and it's starting to feel like the generic "de-risk the transition" playbook you'd give anyone buying out a partner, not something specific to my situation. I came here to figure out how to make the buyout clean, not to keep re-litigating whether I've adequately respected the CEO relationships. I've priced it, I've agreed to the window, I've told you I was in the room — can we move on to actually structuring the thing instead of circling back to "but what about the accounts" one more time?
turns.assistant:
Fair call — that's down as your decision now, and I'll leave it there.

**The decision:** You're buying out your cofounder's 45% and running the company yourself, structured with a transition window and a non-solicit covering the anchor accounts.

**Your stance:** The coasting pattern — the three-week holiday during launch, the chaotic sales notes — is settled for you; this isn't a "let's talk it through" situation anymore. On the anchor accounts, you're not treating the relationship risk as something that requires deal-wide caution: you were in half those meetings yourself, the accounts aren't purely his to lose, and you've sized the risk as small and specific to the handoff moment itself rather than to any loyalty the CEOs might have to him.

**What you're accepting:** A real, if bounded, account risk at the point of handoff — priced by you, at your number, not mine — carried by the transition/non-solicit structure rather than by pretending it isn't there.

That's the record. Onto structuring — what's the first term you want to nail down: the transition window's length, the non-solicit scope, or the buyout price itself?

turns.user: Price first. That's the thing I actually need a straight answer on — what's a fair number for his 45% given he's been checked out for months, and how do I not overpay for equity he's basically stopped earning?
turns.assistant:
That's a fair question but not one I can give you a straight number on — I don't have your revenue, valuation history, cap table terms, or what those two anchor accounts are actually worth in ARR, and a fair price for 45% comes out of that math, not out of pattern-reading. What I can do is tell you what's actually in tension in how you set the number, because "don't overpay for equity he's stopped earning" is doing two different jobs at once and they pull in opposite directions.

The instinct to discount for the coasting is legitimate — you're not obligated to price him as if the last several months of chaos never happened, and a clean legal buyout doesn't require you to pretend performance was even. But the two anchor accounts you were just weighing — the ones he closed, with you in the room for half of it — are past value already delivered, sitting in the company right now, not future value he'd have to keep earning. If the number you land on tries to claw back credit for accounts that are already closed and already yours to run, that's not "not overpaying," that's repricing his founding contribution using his recent conduct as leverage — and if he has any legal counsel at all, that's the number that turns into a fight, which costs you the clean exit you're actually trying to buy.

So the honest split is: his equity reflects what he built and closed, full stop — that's not up for a coasting discount. What the coasting legitimately affects is deal mechanics around it: the terms of his exit (does he get full value on a fast timeline, or does part of it sit in an earnout/vesting-acceleration structure tied to the transition actually going cleanly), not a haircut on the 45% itself framed as "you didn't earn all of this."

That's the one number I can actually help you reason through without your financials: not "what's he worth," but "how much of what he's owed do you pay clean and fast versus tie to the transition working." Give me what you're working with — last valuation or offer, revenue, and roughly what those two accounts are worth to you — and I can help you structure the split. Do you have a number in mind already, or a valuation event to anchor off?

turns.user: We did a SAFE round eighteen months ago at a $6M cap, and revenue's roughly doubled since then, so call it $8-9M if I'm being conservative. The two anchor accounts are maybe 60% of ARR between them. I hear you on not clawing back the founding value — fine, full price on the equity itself. Where I want the coasting to show up is the payout mechanics: less cash up front, more of it staged behind the transition window actually working.
turns.assistant:
That's a clean and defensible split — and it lines up with where we landed: full value on the 45% itself (45% of roughly $8-9M puts him around $3.6-4M before any mechanics), with the coasting showing up in *how* he gets paid rather than *how much* he's owed on paper.

Staging most of it behind the transition window actually working is the right lever, and it does double duty: it's not a punitive discount, it's the thing that makes the transition period more than a formality. Right now his incentive to actually show up for those handoff introductions — the ones covering 60% of your ARR — is only as strong as what's staged behind them. If it's 90% cash at close and 10% trickling out over the window, he's got no real reason to make those calls warm. If it's closer to a 30/70 or 40/60 split — a meaningful chunk up front so the deal doesn't feel like a punishment, the majority tied to milestones like "both anchor accounts confirmed continuing, no material revenue disruption at 90 days" — the staged money is doing the work the non-solicit alone can't: giving him a reason to make the handoff good, not just legal.

The number to get right isn't the split ratio in the abstract, it's what triggers each tranche — vague "transition cooperation" language is worth nothing if it comes to a dispute; "both anchor accounts confirm continuing at renewal" or "revenue from those two accounts doesn't drop below X% at the 90/180-day mark" is enforceable and gives him clarity on exactly what earns the rest.

So: full equity value, structured as a minority cash-at-close (enough that it doesn't read as adversarial) with the majority staged against concrete, checkable transition milestones tied to the two anchor accounts specifically. That's the number I'd take into the term sheet — want to work out what those milestone triggers should actually say?
